modules.title: Present Simple Basics
modules.description: Learn to make sentences in the present simple tense — the most common tense in English. Cover subject-verb agreement, negatives, and questions.

lessons.title: I, You, We, They
lessons.description: Learn how to use the base form of verbs with plural pronouns and 'I'.

body.html:
With the pronouns I, you, we, and they, we use the base form of the verb — no changes needed.

  • I eat breakfast at 8 o'clock.
  • You live near the park.
  • We work in an office.
  • They play football on Saturdays.

The base form is the simplest version of the verb: eat, live, work, play.
tips: Think: I/you/we/they + verb (no change).
'You' is the same for one person and many people in English.

body.question: We ___ English every day.
body.explanation: 'We' takes the base form of the verb. The correct form is 'study'.

body.translation: They drink coffee in the morning.

lessons.title: He, She, It
lessons.description: Learn the third-person singular rule: adding -s or -es to verbs.

body.html:
With he, she, and it, we add -s or -es to the verb.

General rule: add -s

  • She reads books.
  • He works at a hospital.

Verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: add -es

  • He watches TV.
  • She goes to school.

Verbs ending in consonant + y: change y → ies

  • He studies (study → studies).
  • She carries (carry → carries).
tips: Remember: he/she/it = verb + s (or -es).
'Have' is special: he/she/it HAS (not 'haves').

body.explanation: 'Go' ends in -o, so we add -es for he/she/it: 'goes'.

lessons.title: Negative Sentences
lessons.description: Learn to make negative sentences with don't and doesn't.

body.html:
To make a negative sentence in the present simple, use don't or doesn't + the base form of the verb.

I / you / we / they + don't + verb

  • I don't like spicy food.
  • They don't live in London.

He / she / it + doesn't + verb

  • She doesn't work on Sundays.
  • He doesn't eat meat.

Important: After 'doesn't', the verb returns to the base form — no -s!
tips: don't = do not, doesn't = does not.
Common mistake: 'He doesn't likes' ✗ → 'He doesn't like' ✓

body.question: She ___ coffee.
body.explanation: 'She' uses 'doesn't' + base form. 'Doesn't drink' is correct.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.description: Learn to ask yes/no questions with Do and Does.

body.html:
To ask a yes/no question in the present simple, put Do or Does at the start of the sentence.

Do + I/you/we/they + verb?

  • Do you like pizza?
  • Do they live here?

Does + he/she/it + verb?

  • Does she speak French?
  • Does he work here?

Important: After 'Does', use the base form — no -s on the verb!

Short answers

  • Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
  • Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
tips: Question word order: Do/Does + subject + base verb + ...?
Never say 'Does she speaks?' — always base form after does.

body.explanation: 'He' is third-person singular, so we use 'Does' to start the question.

modules.title: Everyday Essentials
modules.description: Build your basic English vocabulary — greetings, numbers, days, months, colors, and shapes you need for everyday life.

lessons.title: Greetings & Introductions
lessons.description: Learn how to say hello, goodbye, and introduce yourself in English.

body.html:
English has different greetings for different times of day and levels of formality.

Saying hello

  • Hello / Hi — any time, any situation
  • Good morning — before 12:00 PM
  • Good afternoon — 12:00 PM to ~6:00 PM
  • Good evening — after ~6:00 PM

Introducing yourself

  • My name is Maria. / I'm Maria.
  • Nice to meet you.
  • How are you? — I'm fine, thank you.

Saying goodbye

  • Goodbye / Bye
  • See you later / See you tomorrow
  • Good night — only when leaving at night or going to sleep
tips: 'Good night' is a goodbye, NOT a greeting. Don't use it to say hello.
'How are you?' is often just a greeting — people expect a short answer like 'Fine, thanks.'

body.question: It's 9:00 AM. You meet your teacher. What do you say?

body.sentence: Hi! My ___ is Anna. Nice to meet you!
body.explanation: The standard introduction phrase is 'My name is [name]'.

lessons.title: Numbers 1–20
lessons.description: Learn to count from 1 to 20 and use numbers for ages and phone numbers.

body.html:
Here are the English numbers from 1 to 20:

1 — one6 — six11 — eleven16 — sixteen
2 — two7 — seven12 — twelve17 — seventeen
3 — three8 — eight13 — thirteen18 — eighteen
4 — four9 — nine14 — fourteen19 — nineteen
5 — five10 — ten15 — fifteen20 — twenty

Using numbers

  • Age: I am twelve years old.
  • Phone numbers: say each digit: 0-7-9-3-5-1-2-8-4-6
  • Quantity: I have three brothers.
tips: 11 and 12 are unique words (eleven, twelve) — not 'oneteen' or 'twoteen'.
13–19 end in '-teen'. The stress is on '-teen': thirTEEN, fourTEEN.

body.explanation: The word for the number 2 is 'two'. Be careful: 'two', 'too', and 'to' sound the same!

lessons.title: Days & Months
lessons.description: Learn the days of the week and months of the year in English.

content.title: Days of the Week & Months of the Year

body.html:
Days of the week

  1. Monday
  2. Tuesday
  3. Wednesday (silent 'd': /ˈwɛnz.deɪ/)
  4. Thursday
  5. Friday
  6. Saturday
  7. Sunday

Months of the year

January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December

Key rules

  • Days and months always start with a capital letter.
  • Use on with days: on Monday, on Friday.
  • Use in with months: in January, in March.
tips: The 'd' in 'Wednesday' is silent. Say: WENZ-day.
In English, the week often starts on Monday (business) or Sunday (calendars).

body.question: My birthday is ___ July.
body.explanation: We use 'in' with months: in July, in March, in December.

lessons.title: Colors & Shapes
lessons.description: Learn the names of basic colors and common shapes.

body.html:
Colors

  • 🔴 red
  • 🔵 blue
  • 🟢 green
  • 🟡 yellow
  • 🟠 orange
  • 🟣 purple
  • ⚫ black
  • ⚪ white
  • 🟤 brown
  • 🩷 pink

Shapes

  • ⬜ square — 4 equal sides
  • ▶ triangle — 3 sides
  • ⬤ circle — round, no sides
  • ▬ rectangle — 4 sides, 2 long and 2 short
  • ⭐ star — has points

Colors go before the noun: a red car, a blue circle.
tips: In English, colors are adjectives and go BEFORE the noun: 'a blue sky' (not 'a sky blue').
'Orange' is both a color and a fruit!

body.question: A shape with three sides is called a ___.
body.explanation: A triangle has exactly 3 sides. 'Tri' means three.

body.sentence: The sky is ___ on a sunny day.
body.explanation: The sky is typically blue on a clear, sunny day.

modules.title: First Phrasal Verbs
modules.description: Phrasal verbs are very common in everyday English. Start with the easiest and most useful ones for daily routines, electronics, and clothing.

lessons.title: Wake Up & Get Up
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs for your morning routine.

body.html:
A phrasal verb is a verb + a small word (particle) that together have a special meaning.

wake up

= to stop sleeping

  • I wake up at 7 o'clock.
  • She wakes up early on weekdays.

get up

= to get out of bed and stand

  • I get up and take a shower.
  • He doesn't get up until 9 on Sundays.

What's the difference?

You can wake up (open your eyes) but stay in bed. When you get up, you leave the bed.
tips: wake up = eyes open; get up = out of bed.
These are separable: 'Wake me up at 7' or 'Wake up at 7'.

body.question: My alarm rings at 6:00, but I ___ at 6:30. (= I leave my bed at 6:30)
body.explanation: 'Get up' means to leave your bed. You wake up when the alarm rings, but you get up later.

body.sentence: I always ___ up early on Monday mornings.
body.explanation: Both 'wake up' and 'get up' work here. 'Wake up' = stop sleeping; 'get up' = leave bed.

lessons.title: Turn On & Turn Off
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs for electronics, lights, and appliances.

body.html:
turn on

= to start a machine, light, or device

  • Turn on the TV, please.
  • She turns on the computer every morning.

turn off

= to stop a machine, light, or device

  • Please turn off the lights.
  • He turns off his phone at night.

Separable phrasal verbs

You can put the object between the verb and the particle:

  • Turn the light on. = Turn on the light.
  • Turn it off. (with pronouns, you MUST separate: not 'turn off it')
tips: With pronouns (it, them), always separate: 'Turn it on' ✓ / 'Turn on it' ✗
Similar: switch on / switch off (more British English).

body.question: The radio is too loud. Please turn ___.
body.explanation: With pronouns, you must separate: 'turn it off'. 'Turn off it' is incorrect.

lessons.title: Put On & Take Off
lessons.description: Learn phrasal verbs for getting dressed and undressed.

body.html:
put on

= to place clothing on your body

  • Put on your jacket — it's cold!
  • She puts on her shoes before leaving.

take off

= to remove clothing from your body

  • Take off your coat when you come inside.
  • He takes off his tie after work.

Separable

Like 'turn on/off', these are separable:

  • Put your hat on. = Put on your hat.
  • Take it off. (pronoun must go in the middle)
tips: put on ≠ wear. 'Put on' = the action of dressing. 'Wear' = having clothes on your body.
'Take off' also means an airplane leaves the ground: 'The plane takes off at 3 PM.'

body.explanation: 'Put on' means to place clothing on your body. 'Put on your raincoat' = wear your raincoat because of the rain.

body.question: You arrive home and it's warm inside. You ___ your coat.
body.explanation: When it's warm and you don't need your coat, you 'take off' your coat (remove it).
